prompt: What kind of thinking does security (red team / blue team) work most reward on a day-to-day basis?
choices: Adversarial thinking -- habitually asking how a system could be abused, not just how it's used
Aesthetic thinking -- judging whether an interface feels pleasant to use
Statistical thinking -- interpreting the significance of experimental results
Spatial thinking -- reasoning about physical sensor placement

prompt: A nightly pipeline silently drops 2% of rows because an upstream API renamed a field. Which habit, central to data engineering, would have caught this earlier?
choices: Writing more unit tests for the UI layer
Adding a data quality / schema check so the failure is loud instead of silent
Switching to a faster database engine
Increasing the server's memory allocation

prompt: Why does game development specifically reward tight iteration loops (tweak-play-tweak) rather than upfront design or formal proof?
choices: Because game engines are too slow to compile code any other way
Because whether a mechanic feels fun is a subjective judgment that only emerges from repeated playtesting, not from specification
Because players refuse to test anything that hasn't been proven correct
Because game studios require daily code reviews by law

prompt: Compared to a fast domain like game dev, what makes ML research's feedback loop distinct?
choices: It's equally fast, just with different tools
It has no feedback loop at all -- results are purely theoretical
It's long (hours to days per experiment) and frequently ends in a negative result that still has to be treated as useful signal
It only provides feedback once a product has shipped to real users

prompt: What makes debugging in robotics/IoT distinct from debugging pure software?
choices: Robotics code never has bugs, only hardware failures
Sensors can drift or give noisy/false readings, and reproducing a bug may require physically observing hardware, with slower feedback loops than rerunning a test
Robotics debugging only happens in simulation, never on real hardware
IoT firmware cannot be debugged with a debugger at all

prompt: In the worked example, Maya ranks Robotics/IoT low and explicitly writes 'no evidence' next to it instead of inventing a reason. Why does the lesson treat this as doing the ranking correctly?

Because an honest ranking should distinguish real evidence from guesses rather than dressing up a guess as a reasoned judgment
Because Robotics/IoT should always be ranked last for every learner
Because admitting a lack of evidence disqualifies a learner from ever trying that branch

As a fixed result that should never be revisited once written down
